capabilities.fallback: No application column: applications are not shown.
No application column: switches cannot be counted.
No stage column → steps are grouped by your business definition; without it, the map has no stage boxes.
No process level columns → no sub-process hierarchy (levels that are missing are skipped).
No action column → milestones (submitted, approved, closed) cannot be detected.
capabilities.needs: an action / completion column (e.g. submitted, approved)

capabilities.fallback: No step-run ID → a run of a step is consecutive events of that step in a case.
No active time or end time → time spent is estimated from gaps between events.
Until a business definition is approved, the order comes from the business, your documents, the AI or the data (page 3).
capabilities.needs: an approved business definition of the process

capabilities.fallback: The summary is written from fixed templates.

data.explain: Score from the order strength (0.91; 0 = steps in any order, 1 = always the same order), weighted by how stable the order is across samples; Low with at most 50 when the strength of all the data (0.91) is below 0.3 or fewer than 25% of cases follow the order (71.8% do).
reasons: the data shows a clear order

inside.reason: Not available: map an Action / UI event column on Import data to see the inside of each step.

subprocess.reason: No Action / UI event column was mapped, so the work inside each step cannot be shown. Map an action column on Import data to see sub-processes.

recommendations.text: Check why 13.3% of the cases reaching Approve Request come back to it after a pause.

summary.text: The analysis covers 400 cases and 2,426 events (data quality score 79 / 100).
The median case takes 2.9 weeks (2.8–3.2); 90% of cases finish within 5.3 weeks.
13.3% of the cases reaching Approve Request return to it later (rework after a pause).
The 10 most common paths together cover 75.0% of cases.

checks.explanation: Rows without a case ID, activity or timestamp cannot be placed in the process.
checks.fix: Ask the data owner why these fields are empty; re-extract with the missing fields filled.
checks.title: 1. Required fields present

checks.explanation: Placeholder dates (before 1990, e.g. 1970-01-01) and future dates are system defaults or errors; they break event order and durations.
checks.title: 2. Timestamps readable and realistic

checks.explanation: When only the date is recorded, the order of steps on the same day is a guess, and waiting times under a day cannot be measured.
checks.title: 3. Time of day recorded

checks.explanation: If two steps have the same time, nobody can tell which came first, so arrows on the map may point the wrong way.
checks.fix: Add seconds or a sequence number to the extract; if one exists, map it on the mapping screen.
checks.shown: 15.6% of events share their time with another event in the same case
checks.title: 4. Event order is clear

checks.explanation: Copies inflate counts and create fake loops (a step that seems to repeat). They are removed automatically before analysis.
checks.fix: Usually caused by joining tables during extraction; check the extract query.
checks.title: 5. No duplicate events

checks.explanation: The same step written two ways (capitals, spaces, typos) appears as two boxes on the map and splits its counts.
checks.fix: Merge the names listed below (the most frequent spelling is first): tick them under this check on page 2 and click Apply merges, then convert again.
checks.title: 6. Activity names are consistent

examples: Usual starts: Create Request, Approve Request, create request
Usual ends: Pay Invoice, Reject Request, Receive Invoice, Cancel Order, Receive Goods
checks.explanation: Cases cut off by the extract window (started before it or still running) look shorter than they really are and add fake paths.
checks.shown: 1.5% of cases (6) start or end unusually
checks.title: 7. Cases have a normal start and end

checks.explanation: One-event cases have no path to analyse. Very long cases often mean a case ID was reused for many different items.
checks.shown: 0.0% of cases have one event; longest case 8 events (99.9% have ≤ 8)
checks.title: 8. Cases have more than one event

checks.explanation: With few cases, a pattern can appear by chance. Results become reliable from about 1,000 cases.
checks.fix: Extract a longer period or more business units.
checks.title: 9. Enough cases

checks.explanation: If almost every case takes its own path, there is no main process to show, and the map becomes 'spaghetti'.
checks.shown: 104 unique paths of events for 400 cases (ratio 0.26; the report counts paths of step runs, with repeated events merged, so it finds fewer); top 10 paths cover 64.8%
checks.title: 10. A dominant process exists

checks.explanation: Built again from different halves of the data, a trustworthy map shows the same main arrows. If it changes, the map is driven by chance.
checks.fix: Add more cases, or reduce variety first (merge labels, focus on one case type).
checks.shown: 0.84 average similarity of the top 31 arrows across 20 half-samples (worst 0.77)
checks.title: 11. The process map is stable

checks.explanation: Only well-filled columns can be used to explain slow or unusual cases.
checks.shown: 5 of 5 extra columns are at least 80% filled
checks.title: 16. Extra columns are filled

checks.explanation: Common in desktop, clickstream and status data: the same step is recorded many times in a row. Each repeat becomes a loop on the map and hides the real flow.
